messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 47
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Park Ranger
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 72

The fever does not break. It is October, and the hospital air is cold and sterile. Elias stands beside the ICU bed, forty-seven years old but suddenly unmoored, watching the intravenous pump drip in a rhythm that feels like a countdown. His daughter’s breathing has grown shallow. The monitors chirp then scream when her saturation dips into the red. A doctor speaks in clipped tones about airway management. Elias holds his wife’s hand until his knuckles whiten, but he cannot look away from the tubes, the machines, the fragile rise and fall of his child’s chest. They pull her back, but the sound of the drip follows him out of the hospital. The first year is a blur of altered time. He wakes before dawn, heart already hammering, convinced the drip has started again somewhere in the house. He checks the hallway three times. He stands outside his son’s bedroom, listening to the inhale-exhale count until his shoulders drop. The house feels too quiet. Quiet feels like a trick waiting to snap. He avoids the pediatric wing when they drive past the medical center, taking long routes through the commercial district. He does not cry at funerals anymore. He stands straight, jaw tight, as if holding everything in keeps it from leaking out. In his family, suffering was met with steady hands and unspoken prayers; now that endurance feels less like strength and more like a cage. The world has split into two categories: safe, and not-yet-safe. He returns to the land, hoping it will reset his pulse. As a park ranger in the coastal highlands, he learns to patrol the upper trails, sticking to the edges, never venturing into dense foliage. He checks every vehicle that pulls into the ranger station lot, noting tire depth, fuel levels, the condition of first-aid kits. He volunteers for night shifts, walking the perimeter with a flashlight, scanning the tree line for movement. He tells himself it is protocol. When a branch snaps, his hand rests on the radio at his hip, breath held until he confirms it is only wind. He used to read the forest like a familiar face. Now he reads it for fractures. A dropped temperature is a signal to mobilize. His body no longer rests even when his eyes are open. His wife, Mei, has learned not to ask if he slept. She leaves glasses of water on the nightstand and sits on the edge of the bed, reading aloud in a soft, steady voice until his breathing matches hers. He loves her, but he cannot tell her about the nights he lies rigid, imagining the beep of a heart monitor turning into the kitchen timer. He flinches when the oven dings. He walks the same loop every morning, eyes tracking the shift of light across the canopy, hands hovering near his belt. When we sit, he tells me about the moss on the north side of the cedars, about the migration of the black bears, about the way the creek swells after rain. He speaks clearly, competently, but his eyes never rest. They keep moving, measuring, waiting. The land he once called home now functions as a checklist of escape routes, and he walks through it like a man who knows exactly how long the ground can hold his weight. He is still on watch.
